lessons.title: i mesi — Rome's own months
lessons.gloss: the months — the Roman calendar, barely worn down

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The months, taken apart until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Sitting next to Rome, Italian kept the month names closest to Latin of all the sisters — the same procession of gods and Caesars, barely worn. And two things you know pay off: marzo is the war-god of martedì, and settembre– dicembre are the Latin numbers 7–10.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 12 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: Italian, from Latin, who / what, Spanish twin. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
The Italian tells: gennaio kept the -aio of Januarius, and settembre/ottobre keep the doubled/assimilated look (ottobre, like otto). And two payoffs land:
marzo = Mars = martedì. The month and Tuesday honour the same war-god — Martius and Martedì. One unlocks the other.
settembre…dicembre = 7…10. Still the Latin numbers, because the Roman year began in March; then luglio (Julius) and agosto (Augustus) were inserted and shifted the count.

segments.instruction: the twelve — "gennaio, febbraio, marzo … novembre, dicembre"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the twelve — "gennaio, febbraio, marzo … novembre, dicembre"]

segments.text: Which god links marzo and martedì? (Mars.) Why is dicembre Latin for "ten"? (The Roman year began in March.) Which two months honour real people? (Luglio — Julius; agosto — Augustus.) Next: the stagioni, the seasons.

lessons.title: le stagioni — the four seasons
lessons.gloss: the seasons — and "primavera," the first green

segments.text: The word for "season," stagione, is itself a small lesson: it's Latin statiō, a "standing" — a fixed station of the year (cousin of English station, stage). And the loveliest of the four, primavera, means the "first green."

utterances: Italian: la primavera (spring). from Latin: prīma vēra. literally: "first spring / first green" (prima "first" + vera from ver "spring").
Italian: l'estate (summer). from Latin: aestas / aestātem. literally: "the heat, the hot season".
Italian: l'autunno (autumn). from Latin: autumnus. literally: "autumn" (twin of English autumn).
Italian: l'inverno (winter). from Latin: hibernum. literally: "the wintry season" (cousin of hibernate).

segments.text: primavera = prima + vera: the "first spring." Latin vēr was the word for spring; Italian (and Spanish, and Portuguese) built "prima-vera," the year's first season — the same idea French once had in primevère.
estate from aestas, "heat." autunno from autumnus, the same word English borrowed. inverno from hibernum "wintry" — English hibernate is "to spend the inverno."

segments.instruction: "stagione from statiō — a 'standing' of the year, like station"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "stagione ← statiō — a 'standing' of the year, like station"]

segments.text: Name the four Italian seasons. (Primavera, estate, autunno, inverno.) What does primavera literally mean? ("First spring / first green.") What Latin word is stagione from, and its English cousin? (Statiō "a standing"; station.) Next chapter builds on this toward family and food.
